unit.title: Energy, aero and performance in 2026
unit.summary: Where the battery gives lap time, when the wings open, and how teams develop the car.

lessons.title: Energy across a lap
lessons.objective: Explain where a car deploys and where it harvests.

payload.prompt: When does a 2026 F1 car harvest the most energy?

options.text: Under braking and on corner exits as the MGU-K recovers power.
options.explanation: Right. Braking is where most energy is recovered; exits are secondary.

options.text: On the straights at full throttle, where the engine feeds power to the battery.
options.explanation: No, straights are where the car deploys. Braking is where it harvests.

options.text: In high-speed corners where downforce is highest.
options.explanation: Energy recovery happens at specific points. Braking is the main one.

options.text: Evenly throughout the lap, always topping up the battery.
options.explanation: No, harvesting is concentrated at braking zones, not constant.

explanation.correct: Right. The MGU-K on the drivetrain recovers braking energy; that is the main harvest point.
explanation.incorrect: A 2026 car harvests most energy under braking via the MGU-K. Corner exits harvest some, but straights are for deploying.

payload.prompt: When does a driver deploy electrical power from the battery?

options.text: On straights and under Overtake Mode to add extra power and speed.
options.explanation: Right. The driver uses the battery power to gain speed on straights and to deploy boost for passing.

options.text: Only in qualifying for a single fast lap.
options.explanation: Deployment happens in both qualifying and racing, with different energy budgets per session.

options.text: Constantly, on every lap, to maintain a high state of charge.
options.explanation: No, deployment is tactical. Drivers choose when to use boost and electrical power.

options.text: When the battery is full, to prevent it from overcharging.
options.explanation: Deployment is about using power for speed, not managing charge levels.

explanation.correct: Right. Drivers deploy electrical power on straights and under Overtake Mode to gain speed and make passes.
explanation.incorrect: Battery power is deployed on straights and under Overtake Mode to add acceleration and top speed.
explanation.sayThisLine: Drivers deploy power on straights and in Overtake Mode.

lessons.title: Clipping and super-clipping
lessons.objective: Explain why a car slows at the end of a straight and what teams do about it.

payload.prompt: What is clipping in a 2026 F1 car?

options.text: The battery is empty, so the car stops accelerating and may even slow as it harvests energy.
options.explanation: Right. Clipping happens when the battery is depleted and cannot provide power.

options.text: A penalty where the wings are clipped for breaking a rule.
options.explanation: No, clipping is not a penalty. It is a battery management issue.

options.text: The active aero wings opening and closing on the straights.
options.explanation: That is wing movement, not clipping. Clipping is about the battery being empty.

options.text: A tactic to save fuel by cutting power at the end of a stint.
options.explanation: Clipping is not a tactic; it is an unwanted slowdown caused by battery depletion.

explanation.correct: Right. Clipping happens when the battery cannot provide power and the car must harvest instead, losing acceleration.
explanation.incorrect: Clipping is when the energy store is empty. The car loses acceleration at the end of a straight and even harvests energy to recharge.

payload.prompt: How do drivers avoid clipping at the end of a straight?

options.text: By lifting off the throttle early and coasting to preserve battery charge for later.
options.explanation: Right. Lift and coast saves energy so the battery does not run empty.

options.text: By using Overtake Mode, which gives instant power and prevents clipping.
options.explanation: No, Overtake Mode uses battery power; it does not prevent clipping.

options.text: By pitting early to reset the battery to full charge.
options.explanation: Pitting does not reset the battery. The strategy must manage energy across the stint.

options.text: By driving in Straight Mode all lap to reduce drag and use less power.
options.explanation: Straight Mode helps efficiency, but lift and coast is the main anti-clipping tactic.

explanation.correct: Right. Lift and coast is the main tactic: ease off early to recharge without losing too much lap time.
explanation.incorrect: Drivers use lift and coast, lifting off the throttle early, to preserve battery energy and avoid clipping.

lessons.title: When to open the wings
lessons.objective: Decide when to hold Straight Mode and when to close it.

statement.speaker: Commentator
statement.text: She is running Straight Mode on the back straight and gains two tenths on him.

options.text: Yes
options.explanation: Right. Low-drag Straight Mode on a long straight gives a speed gain.

options.text: No
options.explanation: Low-drag Straight Mode on a long straight is exactly where you want it for a speed gain.

statement.speaker: Race engineer
statement.text: Keep Corner Mode until the braking zone; do not open the wings yet.

options.text: Yes, high downforce in braking gives grip.
options.explanation: Right. Corner Mode's downforce helps braking and turning.

options.text: No, opening the wings saves fuel and time.
options.explanation: Opening early loses downforce needed for braking. You want high-downforce Corner Mode until the braking zone.

lessons.title: One lap on the battery
lessons.objective: Explain qualifying energy limits and how they shape a lap.

payload.setup: You are a driver in qualifying. The battery has 30% charge left with two corners to go before the main straight. One more deployment would clip you on the straight.
payload.question: Do you deploy Boost now in the corner or save it for the straight?

options.text: Save it for the straight, where it gives more speed gain.
options.explanation: Right. Boost on a long straight gives more lap time than in a corner. Qualifying is about one fast lap.

options.text: Use it now to carry more speed through the corner.
options.explanation: In qualifying, the straight is where lap time is gained. Saving boost for there is smarter than using it in a corner.

payload.translation: In qualifying, you budget electrical power per lap. Long straights are where it matters most.

payload.setup: A driver exhausts the battery on the final straight and clips, losing 0.3 seconds. Had she lifted and coasted earlier, she would have lost only 0.1 seconds but finished with charge to spare.
payload.question: Was the aggressive strategy worth the risk?

options.text: No, the cost of clipping (0.3 seconds) was too high; coasting would have been safer.
options.explanation: Right. Clipping cost more time than coasting would have. Energy management is about the lap total, not just raw power.

options.text: Yes, because she deployed more power overall and that is what matters.
options.explanation: Lap time is all that matters. Clipping cost 0.3 seconds; coasting would have cost only 0.1. The numbers do not favor aggression here.

payload.translation: Energy management is about balancing aggression with the cost of clipping.

lessons.title: Who has the best power unit
lessons.objective: Explain homologation-style upgrades and the ADUO safety net.

payload.prompt: What is PU allocation in F1?

options.text: A limit on how many power-unit elements each team may use per season; extra elements mean a grid penalty.
options.explanation: Right. Teams get a budget of engines, turbos, MGU-Ks and other parts. Exceeding it costs places on the grid.

options.text: The total horsepower each team's engine is allowed to produce.
options.explanation: No, that is a power limit, not an allocation. Allocation is about the number of elements you can use.

options.text: The fuel budget each driver gets for a single race.
options.explanation: That is fuel allocation. PU allocation is about the number of power-unit parts per season.

options.text: A rule allowing any team to request new engines from the FIA if theirs break.
options.explanation: That is not what PU allocation is. It is a limit on how many components you can use per year.

explanation.correct: Right. Each team gets a PU allocation: a set number of each component per season. Fit an extra engine and you take a grid penalty.
explanation.incorrect: PU allocation is a seasonal budget on power-unit elements. Exceed it and you incur grid penalties.
explanation.sayThisLine: PU allocation limits the number of engines and turbochargers per season.

options.text: Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities for engine makers who fall behind, assessed after key rounds.
options.explanation: Right. ADUO gives struggling manufacturers extra upgrade chances to close the gap.

options.text: A penalty for using too many power-unit upgrades in a single season.
options.explanation: No, ADUO is a support measure, not a penalty. It is designed to help struggling suppliers.

options.text: An automatic engine upgrade given to every team at mid-season.
options.explanation: ADUO is not automatic. It is awarded based on performance and applies only to underperforming manufacturers.

options.text: A rule that lets teams share engines with their sister team to save costs.
options.explanation: Sharing is already allowed. ADUO is about extra development opportunities for struggling manufacturers.

explanation.correct: Right. ADUO is a safety net: it checks performance after specific rounds and gives struggling manufacturers extra upgrade tokens to catch up.
explanation.incorrect: ADUO (Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities) is designed to keep new or struggling power-unit makers competitive by granting extra upgrades.
explanation.sayThisLine: ADUO helps struggling manufacturers close the gap with extra upgrades.

payload.prompt: What was the 2026 compression-ratio dispute about?

options.text: Whether engine compression should be measured when the engine is cold or hot, as this affects how powerful it is measured to be.
options.explanation: Right. Some manufacturers wanted cold-only measurement; others argued that hot measurement was fairer because it reflects real racing conditions.

options.text: A rule that all engines must have the same compression ratio to be fair.
options.explanation: No, engines can differ in compression. The row was about how it gets measured and verified.

options.text: A ban on high-compression engines because they are more polluting.
options.explanation: Compression ratio is not about emissions. The row was about measuring standards.

options.text: A debate over whether turbocharged engines should be allowed at all.
options.explanation: Turbos are part of 2026 regulations. The row was about how compression is measured, not whether turbos exist.

explanation.correct: Right. Cold versus hot compression measurement was contentious because it affects whether an engine is legal and competitive.
explanation.incorrect: The 2026 compression-ratio row was about measurement standards: cold-only or cold-and-hot. This affects power certification.
explanation.sayThisLine: The compression-ratio row was about how engines get measured: cold or hot.

payload.prompt: Match each 2026 power-unit concept to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A manufacturer that makes power units: Ferrari, Mercedes, Honda, Audi or Red Bull-Ford in 2026.
Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities for manufacturers that underperform in the championship.
The seasonal limit on power-unit elements; exceeding it brings grid penalties.

distractorDefinitions: A team that supplies power units to customer teams.
A rule that requires all engines to be the same power level.
A budget for fuel costs per race.

explanation.summary: Power-unit landscape in 2026: five suppliers, ADUO safety net for strugglers, allocation limits per team.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ferrari, Mercedes, Honda, Audi and Red Bull-Ford supply power; ADUO helps, allocation limits PU elements.

lessons.title: Aero development and the tunnel time scale
lessons.objective: Explain ATR, flexi-wings and technical directives.

payload.prompt: What are aero testing restrictions (ATR) in F1?

options.text: A sliding scale of wind-tunnel and CFD time; the worse a team finished last year, the more testing it gets.
options.explanation: Right. ATR is a handicap: slow teams get more development time to catch up; fast teams get less.

options.text: A ban on testing aerodynamics changes mid-season.
options.explanation: No, teams can test throughout the year. ATR is about how much time each team gets.

options.text: A rule that all teams must use the same wind-tunnel facility.
options.explanation: Teams have their own tunnels. ATR is about the hours of testing they are allowed.

options.text: A regulation limiting aerodynamic complexity to reduce drag.
options.explanation: That would be a design rule. ATR is about the time budget for testing.

explanation.correct: Right. ATR is a handicap system: the faster you were last year, the fewer wind-tunnel and CFD hours you get this year.
explanation.incorrect: Aero testing restrictions give more wind-tunnel time to slower teams and less to faster teams. It is a competitive balance tool.
explanation.sayThisLine: ATR gives fast teams less testing time, slow teams more. It is a handicap.

payload.prompt: What is a flexi-wing and why do teams use it?

options.text: A wing that bends under load to cut drag while passing static tests, exploiting a loophole.
options.explanation: Right. A flexi-wing is a grey-area tactic: it bends in racing, reducing drag, but the FIA's static tests did not catch it.

options.text: A wing that adjusts angle to optimize speed in different corner types.
options.explanation: That is active aero, not a flexi-wing. Flexi-wings exploit measurement loopholes.

options.text: A wing that is banned and never used, even by accident.
options.explanation: Flexi-wings have been used before and were eventually banned, but only after teams pushed the boundary.

options.text: A wing designed to fail safely if the car crashes.
options.explanation: That is a safety feature. Flexi-wings are about drag reduction through bending.

explanation.correct: Right. A flexi-wing bends in the airstream to reduce drag, gaining speed. It passes static FIA tests but moves in racing.
explanation.incorrect: A flexi-wing is a wing that bends under speed to cut drag, exploiting a loophole between static tests and racing reality.
explanation.sayThisLine: Flexi-wings bend to cut drag. Teams use them until the FIA closes the loophole.

payload.prompt: What is a technical directive (TD) and when is it used?

options.text: An FIA clarification on how a rule will be policed, often used mid-season to close loopholes.
options.explanation: Right. A TD is an interpretation or enforcement update; it is used to close flexi-wing loopholes and similar tactics.

options.text: A penalty issued to a team for breaking the rules.
options.explanation: A TD is not a penalty itself. It is a clarification that may lead to penalties if teams do not comply.

options.text: A permanent rule change voted on by all teams before the season starts.
options.explanation: TDs are issued during the season without needing team votes. They are fast-track clarifications.

options.text: A requirement for all teams to use the same supplier for a component.
options.explanation: That would be a design rule, not a TD. TDs are about interpretation and enforcement.

explanation.correct: Right. A technical directive is the FIA's tool for mid-season rule clarification. It closes loopholes quickly.
explanation.incorrect: A technical directive is an FIA clarification on how rules are policed, issued during the season to address loopholes or tactics.
explanation.sayThisLine: Technical directives are mid-season rule clarifications from the FIA.

payload.prompt: Match each aero regulation tool to its purpose.

pairs.definition: A handicap system giving more wind-tunnel time to slow teams and less to fast teams.
A wing that bends under load to cut drag, exploiting a loophole between static and dynamic testing.
An FIA mid-season clarification of rule interpretation, often closing loopholes like flexi-wings.

distractorDefinitions: A rule limiting the maximum downforce any team may produce.
A penalty for using aero parts that are not FIA-approved.
A system that automatically bans any aero innovation after one year.

explanation.summary: Aero regulation: ATR handicaps by performance; flexi-wings exploit loopholes; TDs close them mid-season.
explanation.sayThisLine: ATR handicaps, flexi-wings exploit, TDs clarify and close loopholes.

lessons.title: The cost cap and how teams spend
lessons.objective: Explain the cap and why it matters to competitiveness.

payload.prompt: What is the purpose of the F1 cost cap?

options.text: To limit team spending and keep racing competitive by preventing the richest teams from dominating through pure budget.
options.explanation: Right. The cost cap is a salary and spending limit per team per year to level the playing field.

options.text: To reduce the total cost of F1 and make it cheaper for everyone.
options.explanation: The cap limits team spending, but it does not make F1 universally cheaper; it just prevents runaway budgets.

options.text: To ensure that all teams design their cars identically.
options.explanation: The cap is about money, not design. Teams still innovate within the budget limit.

options.text: To ban teams with low budgets from competing.
options.explanation: The cap sets a limit; it does not ban teams. Small teams can still race.

explanation.correct: Right. The cost cap (around $215 million per year) levels competitiveness by stopping the richest teams from spending unlimited amounts.
explanation.incorrect: The cost cap is a yearly team spending limit to keep racing competitive. It prevents unlimited budgets from dominating the sport.
explanation.sayThisLine: The cost cap limits spending to keep the grid competitive.

payload.prompt: What does the F1 cost cap cover?

options.text: Engineering, R&D, factory salaries and car development, with major carve-outs for drivers, marketing and hospitality.
options.explanation: Right. The cap counts the core competitive budget but excludes top salaries and certain operational costs.

options.text: Every single expense a team has, including driver salaries, facilities and marketing.
options.explanation: No, the cap has big carve-outs. Driver salaries, marketing and some facilities are not counted.

options.text: Only the cost of manufacturing and shipping the car to races.
options.explanation: The cap is much broader. It includes salaries and R&D, not just manufacturing.

options.text: The cost to the FIA of running each Grand Prix.
options.explanation: That is a different budget. The cost cap is for teams, not for running races.

explanation.correct: Right. The cost cap is roughly $215 million and covers car development, factory staff and R&D, but has carve-outs for driver salaries.
explanation.incorrect: The cost cap covers team R&D and development with carve-outs for top driver salaries, marketing and some hospitality.
explanation.sayThisLine: The cost cap limits team spending on development, with carve-outs for driver salaries.

payload.prompt: Why does a new regulation era matter for the cost cap?

options.text: A new era resets car design, so all teams start fresh with similar development costs, levelling the field.
options.explanation: Right. The cap and new regulations together prevent old-era advantages from carrying over.

options.text: A new era removes the cost cap entirely because the rules are fresh.
options.explanation: No, the cost cap stays. A new era does not suspend budget limits.

options.text: A new era raises the cost cap so teams can develop new cars faster.
options.explanation: The cap amount changes over time, but a new era is not an excuse to raise it significantly.

options.text: A new era only applies to teams that finish in the top five.
options.explanation: Regulation eras apply to all teams. The cost cap applies to all teams.

explanation.correct: Right. A new era resets car development, so big budgets have less advantage. The cap and fresh regulations work together.
explanation.incorrect: A new regulation era resets car design for all teams. Combined with the cost cap, this prevents long-term budget dominance.
explanation.sayThisLine: New eras and the cost cap together reset the grid.

payload.prompt: Estimate the F1 cost cap in millions of dollars per team per year.

explanation.correct: Right. The cost cap is approximately $215 million per team per year, with carve-outs and variations by category.
explanation.incorrect: The F1 cost cap is approximately $215 million per team per year. It has been adjusted over the years but stays in this ballpark.
explanation.sayThisLine: The cost cap is around $215 million per team per year.

lessons.title: Reading pace from practice
lessons.objective: Tell one-lap pace from race pace and spot sandbagging.

payload.setup: On Friday, one team does fast lap after fast lap on fresh tyres with low fuel. Another team does long runs on high fuel, lap after lap. Their times are similar.
payload.question: Who is actually faster for the race?

options.text: The high-fuel team, because long-run pace is closer to race-day conditions.
options.explanation: Right. Long runs on heavy fuel mimic race pace. Low-fuel fast laps do not tell the full story.

options.text: The low-fuel team, because they are faster on a single lap.
options.explanation: Single-lap pace (qualifying pace) is different from race pace. High fuel long runs are the better race predictor.

payload.translation: In practice, watch fuel loads. High-fuel long runs tell you race pace; low-fuel runs tell you qualifying pace.

payload.setup: A top team is running a heavy engine mode, conservative settings and high fuel in Friday practice. They are 1.5 seconds off the pace. By Saturday, they run a few quick laps and are fastest.
payload.question: What happened?

options.text: They were sandbagging on Friday, hiding true pace to mislead rivals about qualifying strength.
options.explanation: Right. Sandbagging is exactly this: running slow in practice to hide your actual pace and confuse rivals.

options.text: They fixed a major car problem overnight, making them much faster.
options.explanation: In parc ferme, teams cannot change the car that much. Sandbagging is a more likely explanation.

payload.translation: Sandbagging is hiding pace in practice to confuse rivals. Watch for teams suddenly jumping up the order on qualifying day.

payload.prompt: In Friday practice, what combination best shows race pace?

options.text: High fuel load and used tyres over many laps, mimicking race degradation.
options.explanation: Right. High fuel plus tyre wear tells you how the car performs on race day.

options.text: Low fuel and fresh tyres, running as fast as possible for a single lap.
options.explanation: That shows qualifying pace (one-lap speed), not race pace.

options.text: Pit stop practice and setup changes, not time at all.
options.explanation: Setup matters, but time data is important too.

options.text: High fuel with fresh tyres, taking it easy to avoid risk.
options.explanation: Easy pace does not show true speed. High fuel plus some tyre wear is better.

explanation.correct: Right. High fuel long runs on slightly used tyres show real race pace; low-fuel quick laps show qualifying pace.
explanation.incorrect: Long runs on high fuel with tyre degradation are the race-pace indicator. Low-fuel quick laps are for qualifying preparation.
explanation.sayThisLine: High fuel + used tyres = race pace. Low fuel + fresh tyres = qualifying pace.

payload.prompt: Why would a team sandbag in practice?

options.text: To hide true pace from rivals and keep them guessing about qualifying speed.
options.explanation: Right. Sandbagging sows confusion: rivals do not know your real pace and may set their cars wrong.

options.text: Because they are actually slow and do not have anything to hide.
options.explanation: Then it would not be sandbagging; it would just be slow pace.

options.text: To save fuel and run out of it on Saturday.
options.explanation: That does not make sense. You want more fuel in practice.

options.text: Because the rules require teams to hide their best setups until qualifying.
options.explanation: There is no such rule. Sandbagging is a team tactic, not a requirement.

explanation.correct: Right. Sandbagging confuses rivals and keeps your best pace secret until it matters: qualifying.
explanation.incorrect: Sandbagging is a competitive tactic to hide true pace from rivals in practice. It gives an advantage in qualifying.
explanation.sayThisLine: Teams sandbag to hide pace and confuse the competition.
